editionTitle: The Swift Programming Language — Swift 6.4 beta

levels.title: Level 1 · Values & Expressions
levels.summary: Build safe Swift foundations by changing real code.

lessons.title: Constants and Variables
lessons.objective: Choose let when a stored value must not change.
lessons.instruction: The daily practice goal stays fixed. Complete the declaration so Swift protects it from reassignment.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. let creates a constant, so dailyPracticeGoal can't be reassigned after initialization.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: var allows reassignment. The goal never changes, so protect the intent with let.
lessons.sourceTitle: The Basics · Declaring Constants and Variables

lessons.title: Type Annotations
lessons.objective: Declare a value's type before assigning its first value.
lessons.instruction: The welcome message is assigned later. Complete the declaration so Swift knows it stores text.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. : String declares that welcomeMessage stores text even before it has an initial value.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Int stores whole numbers, but the later assignment is text. Use String.

lessons.title: Naming Constants and Variables
lessons.objective: Choose a valid Swift identifier when a name includes a number.
lessons.instruction: The number belongs after the first character. Choose the valid name for a lesson counter.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Swift names can't begin with a number, but numbers can appear later.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: 2lesson begins with a number. Move the number after a valid starting character.
lessons.sourceTitle: The Basics · Naming Constants and Variables

lessons.title: Printing Constants and Variables
lessons.objective: Insert a stored value into printed text with string interpolation.
lessons.instruction: Print the current welcome message inside a longer sentence. Choose the expression that inserts the stored value.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. \(welcome) replaces the placeholder with the stored value when Swift builds the string.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: welcome without interpolation prints those letters as fixed text. Wrap the name in \( and ).
lessons.sourceTitle: The Basics · Printing Constants and Variables

lessons.title: Comments
lessons.objective: Mark a one-line note as nonexecutable text with two forward slashes.
lessons.instruction: Keep the reminder in the source without asking Swift to execute it. Choose the line that makes the reminder a comment.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. // starts a single-line comment, so Swift ignores the reminder when compiling the code.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Plain text is treated as code. Start the reminder with // to make it a single-line comment.

lessons.title: Multiline Comments
lessons.objective: Wrap multiple lines of nonexecutable text in a multiline comment.
lessons.instruction: Disable both reminder lines. Choose the delimiters that make the entire block a multiline comment.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. /* starts a multiline comment and */ ends it, so every enclosed line is ignored by the compiler.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: // comments only the line where it appears. Use /* and */ to enclose multiple lines.

lessons.title: Nested Multiline Comments
lessons.objective: Place a complete multiline comment inside another multiline comment.
lessons.instruction: The outer block is already open. Choose the complete inner comment that can be nested before the outer block closes.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Swift allows a complete /* ... */ block to be nested inside another multiline comment.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: The inner block must open with /* and close with */ before the outer block closes.

lessons.title: Semicolons
lessons.objective: Separate two statements written on the same source line.
lessons.instruction: Keep both statements on one line. Choose the separator Swift requires between them.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Swift requires a semicolon between separate statements written on the same line.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: A comma doesn't separate independent statements. Use a semicolon when both statements share one line.

lessons.title: Integers
lessons.objective: Use an integer type for an exact whole-number count.
lessons.instruction: Completed lessons are counted as exact whole numbers. Choose the suitable type.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Int represents whole numbers and integer arithmetic produces exact results within its bounds.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Double represents floating-point values and can approximate results. Use Int for this exact whole-number count.

lessons.title: Fixed-Point Integer Storage
lessons.objective: Represent a fractional quantity by storing its smallest fixed unit as an integer.
lessons.instruction: Store $1.23 as an integer count of cents. Choose the stored value.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Counting cents stores $1.23 as the exact integer 123 with the decimal point understood at a fixed position.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: 1.23 is a floating-point literal and doesn't fit Int. Store the smallest fixed unit: 123 cents.

lessons.title: Integer Bounds
lessons.objective: Read the largest value supported by a specific integer type.
lessons.instruction: Retrieve the highest value UInt8 can store. Choose the correct type property.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. UInt8.max is the maximum value representable by UInt8.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: min returns the lowest supported value. Use max for the upper bound.

lessons.title: Int
lessons.objective: Use Int when an integer doesn't require a specific bit width.
lessons.instruction: The retry count has no external fixed-width requirement. Choose the general-purpose integer type.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Swift recommends Int unless the task requires a specifically sized integer.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Int32 imposes a specific size without a requirement. Use Int for a general-purpose count.

lessons.title: UInt
lessons.objective: Use UInt only when a native-width unsigned integer is specifically required.
lessons.instruction: An external API explicitly requires an unsigned integer with the platform's native width. Choose the matching type.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. UInt is appropriate when the requirement specifically calls for a native-width unsigned integer.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Int is preferred for ordinary integers, but this explicit unsigned native-width requirement calls for UInt.

lessons.title: Floating-Point Numbers
lessons.objective: Use Double for a general-purpose value with a fractional component.
lessons.instruction: The temperature includes a fractional component and has no exact-size requirement. Choose its type.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Double is the general-purpose floating-point type and supports fractional values.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Int can't store a fractional component. Use Double when no exact floating-point size is required.

lessons.title: Floating-Point Approximation
lessons.objective: Recognize that floating-point math rounds to representable values.
lessons.instruction: Choose the accurate expectation for floating-point calculations.

choices.code: round to the nearest representable value.
always produce an exact mathematical result.

lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Floating-point types can't represent every possible value, so calculations can be rounded.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Floating-point math isn't always exact. Results can round to the nearest representable value.

lessons.title: Type Safety
lessons.objective: Provide a value whose type matches its declared storage type.
lessons.instruction: The constant is declared as String. Choose the value that satisfies Swift's type check.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. The String literal matches the declared String type.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: 42 is an Int and doesn't match String storage. Swift reports mismatched types during compilation.
lessons.sourceTitle: The Basics · Type Safety and Type Inference

lessons.title: Type Inference
lessons.objective: Use the type Swift infers for a floating-point literal.
lessons.instruction: Swift infers pi from its literal. Choose the matching type for a second constant that stores pi.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Swift infers Double for an unannotated floating-point literal.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Swift doesn't infer Int from a literal with a fractional component. It infers Double.
lessons.sourceTitle: The Basics · Type Safety and Type Inference

lessons.title: Integer Literal Radices
lessons.objective: Write a binary integer literal with the 0b prefix.
lessons.instruction: Choose the binary literal whose decimal value is 17.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. 0b marks a binary literal, and 10001 in base two equals 17.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: 0b10010 represents 18. The binary representation of 17 is 0b10001.

lessons.title: Exponent Literals
lessons.objective: Use e notation to scale a decimal floating-point literal by a power of ten.
lessons.instruction: Choose the decimal exponent literal whose value is 125.0.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. 1.25e2 multiplies 1.25 by 10 squared, producing 125.0.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: A negative exponent produces 0.0125. Use e2 to multiply by 10 squared.

lessons.title: Readable Numeric Literals
lessons.objective: Use underscores to improve a numeric literal's readability without changing its value.
lessons.instruction: Write one million with Swift's readability separator. Choose the valid literal.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Underscores can group digits without changing the numeric value.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Commas don't format a Swift numeric literal. Use underscores between digit groups.

lessons.title: Integer Conversion
lessons.objective: Explicitly convert differently sized integer values before combining them.
lessons.instruction: Both operands must have the same type. Convert one from UInt8 to UInt16.
lessons.codePrefix:
let twoThousand: UInt16 = 2_000
let one: UInt8 = 1
let total = twoThousand +
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. UInt16(one) creates a UInt16 value, so both addition operands have the same type.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: UInt16 and UInt8 aren't added implicitly. Convert one explicitly with UInt16(one).

lessons.title: Integer to Floating-Point Conversion
lessons.objective: Explicitly convert an integer before combining it with a Double value.
lessons.instruction: Convert the integer operand so both sides of the addition are Double.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Double(three) explicitly converts the Int so it can be added to a Double.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Swift doesn't implicitly convert an Int variable to Double. Use Double(three).
lessons.sourceTitle: The Basics · Integer and Floating-Point Conversion

lessons.title: Floating-Point to Integer Conversion
lessons.objective: Explicitly convert a floating-point value to an integer, truncating its fractional part.
lessons.instruction: Create an Int from pi. Choose the explicit conversion that produces 3.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Int(pi) explicitly converts the Double and truncates its fractional part, producing 3.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Assigning pi directly keeps a Double. Use Int(pi) for explicit truncating conversion.
lessons.sourceTitle: The Basics · Integer and Floating-Point Conversion

lessons.title: Type Aliases
lessons.objective: Define a context-specific alternative name for an existing type.
lessons.instruction: Create AudioSample as another name for UInt16. Choose the declaration keyword.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. typealias defines AudioSample as an alternative name for the existing UInt16 type.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: struct declares a new type. Use typealias to provide another name for UInt16.

lessons.title: Boolean Literals
lessons.objective: Store a logical state with the Bool type and true or false literals.
lessons.instruction: Represent whether onboarding is complete. Choose the Boolean literal.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. true is one of Swift's two Bool values.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: "true" is a String. Remove the quotation marks to use the Bool literal true.

lessons.title: Boolean Conditions
lessons.objective: Provide a Bool expression to an if statement.
lessons.instruction: i is an Int, so compare it to produce the Bool required by if.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. i == 1 evaluates to Bool, which satisfies the if condition.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Swift doesn't treat an Int as Bool. Compare i to produce a Boolean expression.

lessons.title: Tuple Creation
lessons.objective: Group values of different types into one tuple value.
lessons.instruction: Group an HTTP code and message into one compound value. Choose the tuple expression.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Parentheses and a comma create a tuple containing an Int and a String.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: An array requires compatible element types. Use a tuple to group an Int and String directly.

lessons.title: Tuple Decomposition
lessons.objective: Decompose tuple elements into separate constants.
lessons.instruction: Extract both values from httpError. Choose the tuple pattern.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. The tuple pattern binds each element to its own constant.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: One binding receives the entire tuple. Use a two-element tuple pattern to decompose both values.

lessons.title: Ignoring Tuple Elements
lessons.objective: Ignore an unused tuple element with an underscore.
lessons.instruction: Extract only the status code. Choose the pattern that discards the message.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. _ ignores the second tuple element during decomposition.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: The pattern must account for both tuple elements. Use _ for the value you don't need.

lessons.title: Tuple Index Access
lessons.objective: Access an unnamed tuple element by its zero-based index.
lessons.instruction: Read the first tuple element. Choose its index access.
lessons.codePrefix:
let httpError = (404, "Not Found")
let statusCode = httpError
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Tuple element indexes start at zero, so .0 accesses the first value.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: .1 accesses the second element. Use .0 for the first tuple value.

lessons.title: Named Tuple Elements
lessons.objective: Access a tuple element using the name assigned at tuple creation.
lessons.instruction: Read the named status code element. Choose the member access.
lessons.codePrefix:
let response = (statusCode: 200, description: "OK")
let code = response.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Named tuple elements are accessed through their declared element names.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: The tuple has no element named code. Use its declared statusCode name.

lessons.title: Tuple Modeling Scope
lessons.objective: Reserve tuples for simple groups of related values.
lessons.instruction: The model will grow with behavior and many fields. Choose the suitable modeling direction.
lessons.codePrefix: // For a complex growing model, use
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Tuples suit simple groups; complex data should be modeled with a structure or class.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: The source limits tuples to simple groups. Use a structure or class for a complex model.

lessons.title: Optional Types
lessons.objective: Declare a type that can contain a value or no value.
lessons.instruction: Conversion can fail, so convertedNumber may contain an Int or no value. Choose its type.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Int? represents either an Int value or the absence of a value.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Int("123") can fail and therefore returns Int?, not a guaranteed Int.

lessons.title: nil
lessons.objective: Set an optional variable to its valueless state with nil.
lessons.instruction: Remove the response code while preserving its optional type. Choose the assignment value.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. nil represents the absence of a value for an optional.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: An empty String is still a value and doesn't match Int?. Use nil for no value.

lessons.title: Checking for nil
lessons.objective: Compare an optional with nil to determine whether it contains a value.
lessons.instruction: Run the branch only when responseCode contains a value. Choose the Boolean comparison.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Comparing the optional with nil produces the Bool required by if.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: An optional Int isn't a Bool condition. Compare it with nil to test for a stored value.

lessons.title: Optional Binding
lessons.objective: Check and unwrap an optional into a temporary non-optional constant.
lessons.instruction: Run the body only when convertedNumber contains a value. Choose the binding condition.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. if let checks for a value and exposes the unwrapped Int inside the branch.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: An optional isn't a Bool condition. Use optional binding to check and unwrap it.

lessons.title: Shorthand Optional Binding
lessons.objective: Use shorthand binding when the unwrapped value keeps the optional's name.
lessons.instruction: Unwrap number into a new constant with the same name. Choose the shorthand condition.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. if let number is the shorthand form when the unwrapped constant keeps the same name.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: The optional isn't a Bool. Prefix the same name with let to bind it.

lessons.title: Multiple Optional Bindings
lessons.objective: Combine optional bindings and Boolean conditions in one if statement.
lessons.instruction: Separate the second optional binding from the first. Choose the required separator.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Commas separate multiple optional bindings and Boolean conditions in one if condition.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: A semicolon doesn't join optional bindings in an if condition. Use a comma.

lessons.title: Providing a Fallback Value
lessons.objective: Use nil coalescing to unwrap an optional or provide a default value.
lessons.instruction: Use "friend" only when name is nil. Choose the nil-coalescing expression.
lessons.codePrefix:
let name: String? = nil
let displayName = name
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. ?? uses the unwrapped left value when present and the right fallback when nil.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: A single ? marks an optional type. Use ?? to provide a fallback value.
lessons.sourceTitle: The Basics · Providing a Fallback Value

lessons.title: Force Unwrapping
lessons.objective: Access an optional's value when absence represents an unrecoverable invariant failure.
lessons.instruction: The validated invariant guarantees convertedNumber contains a value. Choose the explicit force unwrap.
lessons.codePrefix:
let convertedNumber = Int("123")
let number = convertedNumber
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. ! force unwraps the value; it must be reserved for a guaranteed invariant because nil would terminate execution.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: ? doesn't access the wrapped value here. ! force unwraps, but only when nil is an unrecoverable invariant failure.

lessons.title: Force-Unwrap Failure
lessons.objective: Recognize the result of force unwrapping a nil optional.
lessons.instruction: Choose what happens when the following force unwrap executes.

choices.code: Execution stops with a runtime error.

lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Force unwrapping nil triggers a runtime error; it doesn't synthesize a default value.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Force unwrap doesn't provide a default. Accessing nil with ! triggers a runtime error.

lessons.title: Implicitly Unwrapped Optionals
lessons.objective: Declare an optional that can be implicitly unwrapped after its value is guaranteed.
lessons.instruction: The program structure guarantees this value after initialization. Choose the implicitly unwrapped optional type.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. String! declares an implicitly unwrapped optional.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: String? is an ordinary optional. String! grants implicit force-unwrapping when a non-optional value is required.

lessons.title: Choosing a Safe Optional
lessons.objective: Use an ordinary optional when a value can become nil later.
lessons.instruction: The cached token may become nil during its lifetime. Choose the safe declaration.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Use a normal optional when the value may be nil later so every access handles absence explicitly.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: An implicitly unwrapped optional can trap when nil is accessed. Use String? when nil remains possible.

lessons.title: Memory Safety
lessons.objective: Recognize a memory-safety requirement enforced by safe Swift.
lessons.instruction: Choose the access that satisfies bounds safety.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. A two-element array has valid indexes 0 and 1; bounds safety requires a valid index.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Index 2 is outside a two-element array. Safe access must stay within valid bounds.

lessons.title: Memory-Safety Guarantees
lessons.objective: Identify the guarantees that define safe memory access in Swift.
lessons.instruction: Choose the complete set of memory-safety requirements described by the source.
lessons.codePrefix: // Safe Swift requires values to be

choices.code: initialized, in bounds, within lifetime, and safely overlapped.
read before initialization and accessed at any index.

lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Definite initialization bounds lifetime and thread-safety rules protect memory access.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Reading uninitialized memory or using any index violates Swift's stated safety requirements.

lessons.title: Unsafe API Responsibility
lessons.objective: Recognize the responsibility accepted when using unsafe or unchecked APIs.
lessons.instruction: Complete the accurate statement about APIs named unsafe unchecked or unmanaged.

choices.code: the developer takes responsibility for safety.
the compiler preserves every safety guarantee automatically.

lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Unsafe unchecked and unmanaged APIs transfer safety responsibility to the developer.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Those APIs work outside some automatic guarantees. The developer becomes responsible for safety.

lessons.title: Throwing Functions
lessons.objective: Declare that a function can throw an error.
lessons.instruction: Mark the function as able to throw. Choose the declaration keyword.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. throws in the function declaration tells callers that the function can propagate an error.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: catch handles an error in a do statement. Use throws in a throwing function declaration.

lessons.title: Calling Throwing Functions
lessons.objective: Call a throwing function with try inside a do-catch statement.
lessons.instruction: Call loadData inside the do block. Choose the keyword required before a throwing call.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. try marks a call that can throw, and catch handles an error propagated from the do scope.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: throws belongs in a declaration. Prefix a throwing call with try.

lessons.title: Matching Error Cases
lessons.objective: Handle a specific error case with a matching catch clause.
lessons.instruction: Handle only the notFound error in this clause. Choose the matching catch pattern.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. A catch clause can match a specific error case and run its corresponding recovery code.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: throws belongs to declarations and doesn't match an error here. Use catch with the error case.

lessons.title: Assertions and Preconditions
lessons.objective: Choose a precondition for an essential requirement checked in production builds.
lessons.instruction: A public function must reject an invalid index in debug and production builds. Choose the runtime check.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Preconditions are checked in debug and production builds under normal optimization settings.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Assertions are development checks and aren't evaluated in production builds. Use a precondition for this production requirement.

lessons.title: Debugging with Assertions
lessons.objective: Express a development-time assumption with assert.
lessons.instruction: Check the assumption that age is nonnegative during development. Choose the assertion call.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. assert checks a Boolean development assumption and reports the supplied message when it is false.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: print doesn't enforce an assumption. Use assert for a development-time invariant check.

lessons.title: Enforcing Preconditions
lessons.objective: Enforce a condition that must be true before execution can continue.
lessons.instruction: Require the subscript index to be within the collection. Choose the enforcement function.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. precondition evaluates the requirement and stops execution when it is false.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: assertionFailure unconditionally reports a failed assertion. Use precondition to evaluate this required Boolean condition.

lessons.title: Unimplemented Code Paths
lessons.objective: Use fatalError for a prototype path that must always stop until implemented.
lessons.instruction: Create an unimplemented stub that always stops if reached. Choose the function.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. fatalError always halts execution and can mark an unimplemented prototype path.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Assertions can be removed from production builds and don't return Never here. Use fatalError for an always-stopping stub.

levels.title: Level 2 · Operators & Ranges
levels.summary: Combine values, compare results, and express precise boundaries.

lessons.title: Unary, Binary, and Ternary Operators
lessons.objective: Recognize the ternary conditional operator by its three operands.
lessons.instruction: Choose the operator form that evaluates one of two values from a Boolean condition.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. The ternary conditional operator uses a condition and two result expressions: condition ? first : second.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: && is a binary logical operator. The three-part conditional operator starts with ?.

lessons.title: Assignment Operator
lessons.objective: Update a variable with the value on the right side of an assignment.
lessons.instruction: Replace the stored score with newScore. Choose the assignment operator.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. = assigns the right-hand value to the variable on the left.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: == compares two values and returns a Boolean. Use = to update score.

lessons.title: Assignment Does Not Return a Value
lessons.objective: Use equality rather than assignment as an if condition.
lessons.instruction: Swift doesn't allow assignment as an if condition. Choose the comparison operator that returns Bool.
lessons.codePrefix:
let expected = 7
let actual = 7
if actual
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. == returns a Boolean value that if can evaluate; = doesn't return a value in Swift.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Swift assignment doesn't return a value, so if actual = expected is invalid. Use ==.

lessons.title: Arithmetic Operators
lessons.objective: Select the arithmetic operator that multiplies two values.
lessons.instruction: Calculate the total number of practice minutes. Choose multiplication.
lessons.codePrefix:
let days = 5
let minutesPerDay = 20
let totalMinutes = days
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. * multiplies days by minutesPerDay.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: / divides the left value by the right. Use * to calculate repeated groups.

lessons.title: String Concatenation
lessons.objective: Join two String values with the addition operator.
lessons.instruction: Combine the greeting and name into one String. Choose the supported operator.
lessons.codePrefix:
let greeting = "Hello, "
let name = "Swift"
let message = greeting
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. + concatenates the two String values into one result.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Swift doesn't multiply String values. Use + for String concatenation.

lessons.title: Remainder Operator
lessons.objective: Calculate the value left after integer division.
lessons.instruction: Find the remainder after fitting as many groups of four as possible into nine.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. 9 % 4 returns the remainder 1.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: / calculates a quotient. Use % to return the leftover value.

lessons.title: Remainders with Negative Values
lessons.objective: Determine the sign of a Swift remainder when the dividend is negative.
lessons.instruction: Complete the expected result of Swift's -9 % 4 expression.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Swift returns -1 for -9 % 4; this is remainder behavior rather than mathematical modulo.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: For a negative dividend, Swift's remainder keeps the negative sign here: -9 % 4 is -1.

lessons.title: Unary Minus Operator
lessons.objective: Toggle a numeric value's sign with prefix unary minus.
lessons.instruction: Create minusThree from the positive value three. Choose the prefix operator.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Prefix - toggles the numeric sign, producing -3.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: ! operates on Boolean logic. Use prefix - to toggle a number's sign.

lessons.title: Unary Plus Operator
lessons.objective: Recognize that unary plus returns its numeric operand unchanged.
lessons.instruction: Keep minusSix unchanged while writing it with an explicit unary sign.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Unary + returns minusSix without changing its value.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Unary - would toggle -6 to 6. Unary + leaves the value unchanged.

lessons.title: Compound Assignment Operators
lessons.objective: Combine addition and assignment with +=.
lessons.instruction: Increase a by two and store the result back in a. Choose the compound operator.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. a += 2 is shorthand for a = a + 2 and leaves a equal to 3.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: == compares values and doesn't update a. Use += to add and assign in one operation.

lessons.title: Comparison Operators
lessons.objective: Choose a comparison that returns true when two values differ.
lessons.instruction: Check that the current score isn't equal to the previous score.
lessons.codePrefix:
let current = 9
let previous = 7
let changed = current
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. != returns true when its operands aren't equal.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: == returns true only when both values are equal. Use != to detect a change.

lessons.title: Tuple Comparison Order
lessons.objective: Apply Swift's left-to-right tuple comparison.
lessons.instruction: Complete the result. Swift decides this comparison from the first unequal pair of elements.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. The first elements decide the result because 1 is less than 2; the strings aren't compared.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Tuple comparison stops at the first unequal elements. 1 < 2 makes the whole comparison true.

lessons.title: Comparable Tuple Elements
lessons.objective: Use ordered tuple comparison only when the operator supports every paired element.
lessons.instruction: Choose the tuple comparison whose element types all support the less-than operator.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Both String and Int support <, so Swift can compare the tuple elements in order.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Bool doesn't support <, so a tuple containing Bool can't use this ordered comparison.

lessons.title: Ternary Conditional Operator
lessons.objective: Select one of two expressions from a Boolean condition.
lessons.instruction: Add 50 when the row has a header and 20 otherwise. Complete the concise conditional expression.
lessons.codePrefix:
let contentHeight = 40
let hasHeader = true
let rowHeight = contentHeight + (hasHeader
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. condition ? first : second evaluates exactly one of the two result expressions.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: ?? provides a fallback for an optional. Use ? and : for the ternary conditional operator.

lessons.title: Lazy Nil-Coalescing Fallback
lessons.objective: Recognize that a nil-coalescing fallback isn't evaluated when the optional contains a value.
lessons.instruction: The preferred color contains a value. Choose the expression that returns it without evaluating makeDefaultColor().
lessons.codePrefix:
let preferred: String? = "green"
let color = preferred
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. ?? unwraps preferred and doesn't evaluate the fallback when the left side is non-nil.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: || combines Boolean values. Use ?? for an optional fallback with short-circuit evaluation.

lessons.title: Closed Range Operator
lessons.objective: Create a range that includes both its lower and upper bounds.
lessons.instruction: Iterate from one through five, including five. Choose the closed range operator.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. 1...5 includes both 1 and 5.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: 1..<5 excludes 5. Use ... when both bounds belong in the range.

lessons.title: Half-Open Range Operator
lessons.objective: Create a range that includes its lower bound and excludes its upper bound.
lessons.instruction: Iterate over every valid zero-based array index without including names.count.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. 0..<names.count stops before count, matching the final valid index.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: A closed range would include names.count, which is outside the array's valid indices. Use ..<.

lessons.title: One-Sided Range to the End
lessons.objective: Slice from a starting index through the end of a collection.
lessons.instruction: Select every name from index two through the end. Choose the one-sided range.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. 2... starts at index two and continues through the collection's end.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: ...2 selects from the beginning through index two. Put 2 before ... to select the suffix.

lessons.title: One-Sided Range Before a Bound
lessons.objective: Slice from a collection's start while excluding the final bound.
lessons.instruction: Select names before index two, excluding the element at index two.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. ..<2 starts at the collection's beginning and excludes index two.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: ...2 includes the value at index two. Use ..<2 to stop before it.

lessons.title: Testing a One-Sided Range
lessons.objective: Check whether a value belongs to a one-sided range.
lessons.instruction: Create the range containing every value through five, then verify that four belongs to it.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. ...5 contains values less than or equal to five, including four.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: 5... contains values from five upward, so it excludes four. Use ...5.

lessons.title: Logical NOT Operator
lessons.objective: Invert a Boolean value with prefix !.
lessons.instruction: Print the denial message only when entry isn't allowed.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. ! inverts false to true, so the if body runs.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: - changes a numeric sign. Use ! to invert a Boolean value.

lessons.title: Logical AND Operator
lessons.objective: Require two Boolean conditions to both be true.
lessons.instruction: Allow access only when both checks pass.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. && is true only when both Boolean operands are true.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: || needs only one true operand. Use && when both checks are required.

lessons.title: Logical OR Operator
lessons.objective: Accept either of two Boolean conditions.
lessons.instruction: Allow access when the user has a key or knows the override password.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. || is true when either Boolean operand is true.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: && requires both conditions. Use || when either condition is sufficient.

lessons.title: Combining Logical Operators
lessons.objective: Combine required checks with alternative access paths.
lessons.instruction: Require both scans together, while also accepting either backup credential. Choose the missing operator.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. The completed scan pair, key, and password are alternative paths, so they are joined with ||.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: && would require the scan pair and the key. Join alternative access paths with ||.

lessons.title: Explicit Parentheses
lessons.objective: Group a compound Boolean expression to make its intent clear.
lessons.instruction: Group the two required scan checks as one access path before the OR alternatives.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Parentheses make the required scan pair an explicit grouped access path without changing the result.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: The scans must both pass together. Group enteredDoorCode && passedRetinaScan in parentheses.

levels.title: Level 3 · Text & Unicode
levels.summary: Build Unicode-correct text and navigate it with String.Index.

lessons.title: String and NSString Bridging
lessons.objective: Recognize the Foundation class bridged with Swift String.
lessons.instruction: Choose the Foundation class that bridges with Swift String.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Swift String bridges with Foundation's NSString class.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: NSMutableString is the mutable Foundation string class. Swift String bridges with NSString.
lessons.sourceTitle: Strings and Characters · String and NSString Bridging

lessons.title: String Literals
lessons.objective: Create a String value from a double-quoted literal.
lessons.instruction: Initialize the message with text. Choose the valid String literal.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. A String literal is a sequence of characters surrounded by double quotation marks.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Unquoted text is parsed as identifiers and punctuation. Surround a String literal with double quotes.

lessons.title: Multiline String Literals
lessons.objective: Create a String whose value spans multiple lines.
lessons.instruction: Choose the delimiter that preserves the two source lines as one multiline String.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Three double quotes delimit a multiline String literal.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: A single double quote starts a one-line literal. Use three double quotes for multiline text.
lessons.sourceTitle: Strings and Characters · Multiline String Literals

lessons.title: Soft-Wrapping Multiline Text
lessons.objective: Wrap multiline source without adding a line break to the String value.
lessons.instruction: Continue the sentence on the next source line without inserting a newline into the resulting String.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. A backslash at the source line's end suppresses that line break in the String value.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: \n adds a line feed. Use a trailing backslash to soft-wrap source without changing the value.
lessons.sourceTitle: Strings and Characters · Multiline String Literals

lessons.title: String Escape Sequences
lessons.objective:
Insert a line feed with the 
 escape sequence.
lessons.instruction: Place the second word on a new line inside a single-line String literal.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. \n represents a line feed inside a String literal.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: \t inserts a horizontal tab. Use \n for a new line.
lessons.sourceTitle: Strings and Characters · Special Characters in String Literals

lessons.title: Unicode Scalar Escapes
lessons.objective: Write a Unicode scalar value with hexadecimal escape syntax.
lessons.instruction: Create the black-heart character from scalar U+2665.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Swift writes a Unicode scalar as \u{ followed by one to eight hexadecimal digits and }.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Swift's Unicode scalar escape requires braces around the hexadecimal number: \u{2665}.
lessons.sourceTitle: Strings and Characters · Special Characters in String Literals

lessons.title: Extended String Delimiters
lessons.objective: Preserve backslash sequences as literal text with extended delimiters.
lessons.instruction: Create one line containing the characters \n instead of interpreting them as a line feed.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. The surrounding # delimiters prevent \n from invoking its normal escape effect.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: A normal String literal interprets \n as a line feed. Surround the quoted literal with matching # signs.
lessons.sourceTitle: Strings and Characters · Extended String Delimiters

lessons.title: Interpolation with Extended Delimiters
lessons.objective: Match extended-delimiter number signs to enable interpolation.
lessons.instruction: Interpolate the product inside a String surrounded by one # delimiter.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. One # after the backslash matches the literal's one-# extended delimiter and enables interpolation.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Inside a one-# extended literal, ordinary \(...) remains text. Use \#(...).

lessons.title: Initializing an Empty String
lessons.objective: Create an empty String with initializer syntax.
lessons.instruction: Start with an empty mutable String that can be built later.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. String() creates the same empty value as the literal "".
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Use String() to initialize an empty String value.
lessons.sourceTitle: Strings and Characters · Initializing an Empty String

lessons.title: Checking for an Empty String
lessons.objective: Read the Boolean isEmpty property.
lessons.instruction: Run the branch only when output contains no characters.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. isEmpty returns the Boolean value required by if.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: count returns an integer. Use isEmpty for a direct Boolean emptiness check.
lessons.sourceTitle: Strings and Characters · Initializing an Empty String

lessons.title: String Mutability
lessons.objective: Declare a String variable when its value must change.
lessons.instruction: The message is extended after initialization. Choose the declaration that permits mutation.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. var permits the String value to change after initialization.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: A let-bound String can't be reassigned. Use var when the value must mutate.

lessons.title: Strings Are Value Types
lessons.objective: Recognize that assigning a String produces independent value semantics.
lessons.instruction: Mutating the second variable must not change the first. Choose the resulting original value.
lessons.codePrefix:
var original = "Swift"
var copy = original
copy += " 6"
let originalResult =
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. String has value semantics, so mutating copy doesn't mutate original.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: The assignment gives independent String value semantics. original remains "Swift".
lessons.sourceTitle: Strings and Characters · Strings Are Value Types

lessons.title: Iterating over Characters
lessons.objective: Traverse a String as Character values with for-in.
lessons.instruction: Print each extended grapheme cluster in the String separately.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. for-in iterates a String's Character values, including 🐶 as one Character.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Use in to bind each Character produced by the String iteration.
lessons.sourceTitle: Strings and Characters · Working with Characters

lessons.title: Character Type Annotation
lessons.objective: Create a standalone Character from a single-character literal.
lessons.instruction: Declare the exclamation mark as Character rather than inferred String.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. The explicit Character annotation creates a standalone Character value.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: String represents a sequence of characters. Use Character for this single grapheme cluster.
lessons.sourceTitle: Strings and Characters · Working with Characters

lessons.title: Building a String from Characters
lessons.objective: Construct a String from an array of Character values.
lessons.instruction: Convert the Character array into one String.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. String's initializer combines the Character sequence into one text value.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Character represents one grapheme cluster. Use String to combine the full Character array.
lessons.sourceTitle: Strings and Characters · Working with Characters

lessons.title: Appending a String
lessons.objective: Append one String value to a mutable String with +=.
lessons.instruction: Extend instruction with the second String and store the combined result.
lessons.codePrefix:
var instruction = "look over"
let place = " there"
instruction
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. += concatenates place and assigns the result back to instruction.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: == compares the Strings without changing instruction. Use += to append and assign.
lessons.sourceTitle: Strings and Characters · Concatenating Strings and Characters

lessons.title: Appending a Character
lessons.objective: Append one Character to a mutable String.
lessons.instruction: Add the exclamation Character to the end of welcome.

var welcome = "hello"
let mark: Character = "!"
welcome.

lessons.sourceTitle: Strings and Characters · Concatenating Strings and Characters

lessons.title: Multiline Concatenation Boundaries
lessons.objective: Preserve a line break when concatenating multiline String fragments.
lessons.instruction: Choose the first fragment whose value ends with a line feed, keeping three on its own line after concatenation.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. The blank final content line makes start end with a line feed, so three stays on a new line.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Without a final line feed, the last line of start joins directly with the first line of end.
lessons.sourceTitle: Strings and Characters · Concatenating Strings and Characters

lessons.title: Unicode Scalar Values
lessons.objective: Identify a character's Unicode scalar notation.
lessons.instruction: Choose the scalar notation for LATIN SMALL LETTER A.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. U+0061 is the Unicode scalar value for LATIN SMALL LETTER A.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: U+1F425 represents FRONT-FACING BABY CHICK. The scalar for lowercase a is U+0061.
lessons.sourceTitle: Strings and Characters · Unicode Scalar Values

lessons.title: Extended Grapheme Clusters
lessons.objective: Recognize that one Character can contain multiple Unicode scalars.
lessons.instruction: Complete the result. Both values render as é and each forms one Swift Character.
lessons.codePrefix:

let decomposed: Character = "\u{65}\u{301}"
let sameCharacter = precomposed == decomposed
let expected =

lessons.incorrectFeedback: Different scalar sequences can form the same extended grapheme cluster. These Character values are canonically equivalent.
lessons.sourceTitle: Strings and Characters · Extended Grapheme Clusters

lessons.title: Regional Indicator Grapheme Clusters
lessons.objective: Treat a paired regional-indicator sequence as one Character.
lessons.instruction: Declare the two-scalar United States flag sequence as one Swift Character.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. The two regional indicators combine into one extended grapheme cluster and one Character.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: The pair forms a single human-readable flag grapheme cluster, so its Swift type can be Character.
lessons.sourceTitle: Strings and Characters · Extended Grapheme Clusters

lessons.title: Counting Characters
lessons.objective: Count a String's extended grapheme clusters.
lessons.instruction: Read the number of Swift Character values in the text.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. String.count counts extended grapheme clusters rather than encoding code units.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: utf8.count counts UTF-8 code units. Use String.count for human-readable Character values.

lessons.title: Combining Scalars and Character Count
lessons.objective: Predict character count after adding a combining scalar.
lessons.instruction: Append COMBINING ACUTE ACCENT to cafe and choose the resulting Character count.
lessons.codePrefix:
var word = "cafe"
word.append("\u{301}")
let result = word.count
let expected =
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. The combining accent joins the final e, so the String still contains four Character values.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: String.count measures grapheme clusters, not scalar count. The accent combines with e, leaving four Characters.

lessons.title: The First String Index
lessons.objective: Access a String's first Character with startIndex.
lessons.instruction: Read the G at the beginning of greeting using its valid index type.
lessons.codePrefix:
let greeting = "Guten Tag!"
let first = greeting[greeting.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. startIndex identifies the position of the first Character.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: endIndex is the position after the final Character and can't be used as a String subscript. Use startIndex.

lessons.title: The Last Valid String Index
lessons.objective: Move before endIndex to access the final Character.
lessons.instruction: Read the final exclamation mark. Choose the valid index expression.
lessons.codePrefix:
let greeting = "Guten Tag!"
let last = greeting[
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. endIndex is after the last Character, so index(before:) produces the last valid subscript.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: endIndex itself isn't a valid subscript. Move one position before it.

lessons.title: Offsetting a String Index
lessons.objective: Move a String.Index by a character offset.
lessons.instruction: Find the index seven Characters after the start without using an integer subscript.
lessons.codePrefix:
let greeting = "Guten Tag!"
let index = greeting.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. index(_:offsetBy:) advances from a valid String.Index by Character boundaries.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: distance reports the separation between indices. Use index(_:offsetBy:) to create the target index.

lessons.title: String.Index Instead of Integer Subscripts
lessons.objective: Avoid invalid integer indexing for Unicode text.
lessons.instruction: Choose the valid way to read the first Character of a String.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Swift String uses String.Index because Characters can occupy different encoding lengths.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: String doesn't support integer subscripts. Use a String.Index such as startIndex.

lessons.title: Iterating String Indices
lessons.objective: Traverse every valid Character index in a String.
lessons.instruction: Choose the collection of valid String indices for the loop.
lessons.codePrefix:
let greeting = "Hi!"
for index in greeting.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. indices supplies every valid index for subscripting the String.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: endIndex is one position and isn't itself subscriptable. Use indices for the valid sequence.

lessons.title: Inserting a Character
lessons.objective: Insert one Character at a specific String.Index.
lessons.instruction: Place an exclamation mark at the end of welcome.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. insert(_:at:) adds one Character at the specified index.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: remove(at:) deletes a Character. Use insert(_:at:) to add one.
lessons.sourceTitle: Strings and Characters · Inserting and Removing

lessons.title: Inserting String Contents
lessons.objective: Insert another String's contents at a String.Index.
lessons.instruction: Insert " there" immediately before the final exclamation mark.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. insert(contentsOf:at:) adds the full String contents at the selected index.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: append adds only at the end and doesn't accept this index. Use insert(contentsOf:at:).
lessons.sourceTitle: Strings and Characters · Inserting and Removing

lessons.title: Removing a Character
lessons.objective: Remove one Character at a valid String.Index.
lessons.instruction: Delete the final exclamation mark.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. remove(at:) deletes and returns the Character at the supplied index.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: insert(_:at:) adds a Character. Use remove(at:) to delete the existing one.
lessons.sourceTitle: Strings and Characters · Inserting and Removing

lessons.title: Removing a String Range
lessons.objective: Delete multiple Characters with removeSubrange(_:).
lessons.instruction: Remove everything from the first space through the end of welcome.
lessons.codePrefix:
var welcome = "hello there"
let space = welcome.firstIndex(of: " ")!
let range = space..<welcome.endIndex
welcome.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. removeSubrange(_:) deletes all Characters in the supplied range.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: remove(at:) accepts one index. Use removeSubrange(_:) for a range of Characters.
lessons.sourceTitle: Strings and Characters · Inserting and Removing

lessons.title: Substring Results
lessons.objective: Recognize that slicing a String produces Substring.
lessons.instruction: Choose the inferred type of beginning after slicing greeting.
lessons.codePrefix:

let comma = greeting.firstIndex(of: ",")!
let beginning = greeting[..<comma]
let type:
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. A String slice is Substring, which provides String-like operations while sharing storage.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: String slicing returns Substring rather than a new independently stored String.

lessons.title: Storing Substring Results
lessons.objective: Convert a temporary Substring to String for long-term storage.
lessons.instruction: Create independently stored text from beginning before retaining it.
lessons.codePrefix:
let beginning: Substring = greeting.prefix(5)
let stored =
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. String(beginning) creates independent String storage suitable for long-term retention.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: The slice can contain multiple Characters. Convert it with String(_:).

lessons.title: Canonical String Equality
lessons.objective: Compare canonically equivalent Unicode text.
lessons.instruction: Complete the expected result for two scalar representations of café.
lessons.codePrefix:
let precomposed = "caf\u{E9}"
let decomposed = "caf\u{65}\u{301}"
let equal = precomposed == decomposed
let expected =
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Swift equality compares canonically equivalent extended grapheme clusters as equal.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Different scalar sequences can have the same linguistic meaning and appearance. These Strings compare equal.

lessons.title: Visually Similar Unicode Characters
lessons.objective: Distinguish visually similar scalars with different linguistic meaning.
lessons.instruction: Compare Latin A with Cyrillic А and choose the result.
lessons.codePrefix:
let latin: Character = "\u{0041}"
let cyrillic: Character = "\u{0410}"
let equal = latin == cyrillic
let expected =

lessons.incorrectFeedback: Visual similarity doesn't make these characters canonically equivalent. Latin A and Cyrillic А compare unequal.

lessons.title: Testing a String Prefix
lessons.objective: Check the start of a String with hasPrefix(_:).
lessons.instruction: Detect whether the scene belongs to Act 1.
lessons.codePrefix:
let scene = "Act 1 Scene 2"
let isActOne = scene.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. hasPrefix(_:) compares the String's beginning with the supplied text.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: hasSuffix(_:) checks the end. Use hasPrefix(_:) for the opening text.

lessons.title: Testing a String Suffix
lessons.objective: Check the end of a String with hasSuffix(_:).
lessons.instruction: Detect whether the location ends with mansion.
lessons.codePrefix:
let location = "Capulet's mansion"
let isMansion = location.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. hasSuffix(_:) compares the String's ending with the supplied text.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: hasPrefix(_:) checks the beginning. Use hasSuffix(_:) for the final text.
lessons.sourceTitle: Strings and Characters · Prefix and Suffix Equality

lessons.title: UTF-8 Representation
lessons.objective: Access a String as unsigned 8-bit code units.
lessons.instruction: Choose the view that produces UInt8 code units for storage or transmission.
lessons.codePrefix:
let text = "Dog‼🐶"
for codeUnit in text.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. String.utf8 is a collection of UInt8 code units.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: utf16 produces UInt16 code units. Use utf8 for 8-bit units.

lessons.title: UTF-16 Representation
lessons.objective: Access a String as unsigned 16-bit code units.
lessons.instruction: Choose the view that represents text as UInt16 code units.
lessons.codePrefix:
let text = "Dog‼🐶"
for codeUnit in text.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. String.utf16 is a collection of UInt16 code units and can represent some scalars with surrogate pairs.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: utf8 produces UInt8 bytes. Use utf16 for UInt16 code units.

lessons.title: Unicode Scalar Representation
lessons.objective: Access the Unicode scalar values that compose a String.
lessons.instruction: Iterate over UnicodeScalar values and read each 21-bit value as UInt32.
lessons.codePrefix:

levels.title: Level 4 · Collections

lessons.title: Collection Mutability
lessons.objective: Choose var when a collection's membership must change.
lessons.instruction: The list receives another item after initialization. Choose the mutable declaration.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. var permits adding, removing, or replacing collection elements.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: A let-bound collection can't change its membership. Use var for this mutation.

lessons.title: Array and NSArray Bridging
lessons.objective: Recognize the Foundation class bridged with Swift Array.
lessons.instruction: Choose the Foundation class that bridges with Swift Array.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Swift Array bridges with Foundation's NSArray class.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: NSSet represents a set. Swift Array bridges with NSArray.

lessons.title: Array Type Shorthand
lessons.objective: Declare an Array with [Element] shorthand syntax.
lessons.instruction: Declare an ordered collection that stores only Int values.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. [Int] is shorthand for Array<Int>.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Set<Int> stores unique unordered values. Use [Int] for an Array.

lessons.title: Creating an Empty Array
lessons.objective: Initialize an empty Array while preserving its element type.
lessons.instruction: Create an empty Array of Int values.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. [Int]() supplies the element type even though there are no initial values.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: An empty literal alone doesn't provide enough type context here. Initialize [Int]().

lessons.title: Arrays with a Default Value

lessons.title: Adding Arrays Together
lessons.objective: Concatenate Arrays whose element types match.
lessons.instruction: Create one six-element Array from the two three-element Arrays.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. + concatenates Arrays with compatible element types.

lessons.title: Array Literals
lessons.objective: Create an Array from comma-separated values in square brackets.
lessons.instruction: Initialize the shopping list with two String elements.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Square brackets with comma-separated values form an Array literal.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: A colon creates a key-value pair. Use comma-separated String values for an Array.

lessons.title: Reading Array Count

lessons.instruction: Complete the property access that returns two.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. count returns the number of Array elements.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: isEmpty returns Bool. Use count for the number of elements.

lessons.title: Appending an Array Element
lessons.objective: Add one element to an Array's end.
lessons.instruction: Add Flour after the current shopping-list items.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. append(_:) adds one compatible element at the Array's end.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: removeLast() deletes the final element. Use append(_:) to add Flour.

lessons.title: Array Subscripts
lessons.objective: Access the first Array element with zero-based indexing.
lessons.instruction: Read Eggs from the first position.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Array indices start at zero, so index 0 reads the first element.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Index 1 is the second element. Use 0 for the first.
lessons.sourceTitle: Collection Types · Accessing and Modifying an Array

lessons.title: Replacing an Array Subrange
lessons.objective: Replace multiple Array elements through a range subscript.
lessons.instruction: Replace indices one through two with one new item.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. A range subscript replaces all selected elements and may change the Array's count.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: A single index replaces one element with one element. Use the range 1...2.
lessons.sourceTitle: Collection Types · Accessing and Modifying an Array

lessons.title: Inserting and Removing Array Elements
lessons.objective: Insert at an index and remove the element at that index.
lessons.instruction: Choose the call that inserts Maple Syrup at the beginning.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. insert(_:at:) shifts later elements and stores the new value at index zero.

lessons.sourceTitle: Collection Types · Accessing and Modifying an Array

lessons.title: Enumerating an Array
lessons.objective: Iterate with both each element's index and value.
lessons.instruction: Choose the method that supplies (index, value) pairs.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. enumerated() yields a zero-based offset paired with each element.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: sorted() reorders comparable elements. Use enumerated() for index-value pairs.
lessons.sourceTitle: Collection Types · Iterating Over an Array

lessons.title: Set and NSSet Bridging
lessons.objective: Recognize the Foundation class bridged with Swift Set.
lessons.instruction: Choose the Foundation class that bridges with Swift Set.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Swift Set bridges with Foundation's NSSet class.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: NSArray represents an ordered collection. Swift Set bridges with NSSet.
lessons.sourceTitle: Collection Types · Set and NSSet Bridging

lessons.title: Hashable Set Elements
lessons.objective: Use Hashable values as Set elements.
lessons.instruction: Choose the constraint required for a custom value stored in Set.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Set requires Hashable elements so it can determine stable membership and equality.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Comparable supplies ordering. Set membership requires Hashable.
lessons.sourceTitle: Collection Types · Hash Values for Set Types

lessons.title: Set Type Syntax
lessons.objective: Declare a Set with Set<Element> syntax.
lessons.instruction: Declare unique String genres without an ordering contract.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Set<String> stores unique String values.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: [String] is an ordered Array and can contain duplicates. Use Set<String>.

lessons.title: Creating an Empty Set
lessons.objective: Initialize an empty Set with an explicit element type.
lessons.instruction: Create an empty Set of Character values.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Set<Character>() creates an empty Set whose elements are Character.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: [Character]() creates an Array. Use Set<Character>() for unique membership.
lessons.sourceTitle: Collection Types · Creating and Initializing an Empty Set

lessons.title: Set Literals
lessons.objective: Initialize a Set from array-literal syntax with explicit Set context.
lessons.instruction: Create a Set that removes duplicate genres by membership.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. The Set<String> context interprets the literal as unique String membership.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: [String] retains both Rock entries. Use Set<String> for uniqueness.
lessons.sourceTitle: Collection Types · Creating a Set with an Array Literal

lessons.title: Inserting into a Set
lessons.objective: Add a member to a mutable Set.
lessons.instruction: Add Jazz to the favorite genres.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. insert(_:) adds a Set member if it isn't already present.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Set has no ordered end for append. Use insert(_:) to add membership.
lessons.sourceTitle: Collection Types · Accessing and Modifying a Set

lessons.title: Removing from a Set
lessons.objective: Handle the optional value returned when removing Set membership.
lessons.instruction: Remove Rock and enter the branch only if the member existed.
lessons.codePrefix:
var genres: Set = ["Rock", "Jazz"]
if let removed = genres.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. remove(_:) returns the removed element or nil when it wasn't present.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: contains(_:) returns Bool and doesn't mutate the Set. Use remove(_:).
lessons.sourceTitle: Collection Types · Accessing and Modifying a Set

lessons.title: Testing Set Membership
lessons.objective: Check membership with contains(_:).
lessons.instruction: Produce true when Funk is already a favorite genre.
lessons.codePrefix:
let genres: Set = ["Funk", "Jazz"]
let likesFunk = genres.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. contains(_:) returns whether the Set includes that member.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: remove(_:) mutates and returns an optional. Use contains(_:) for a Boolean check.
lessons.sourceTitle: Collection Types · Accessing and Modifying a Set

lessons.title: Ordered Set Iteration
lessons.objective: Create deterministic ordered iteration from an unordered Set.
lessons.instruction: Print the comparable genres in ascending order.
lessons.codePrefix:
let genres: Set = ["Rock", "Jazz"]
for genre in genres.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. sorted() returns an ordered Array for deterministic iteration.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: enumerated() pairs the Set's current iteration order with offsets. Use sorted() for ascending order.
lessons.sourceTitle: Collection Types · Iterating Over a Set

lessons.title: Set Union and Intersection
lessons.objective: Choose the members shared by two Sets.
lessons.instruction: Return only digits found in both oddDigits and primes.
lessons.codePrefix:
let oddDigits: Set = [1, 3, 5, 7, 9]
let primes: Set = [2, 3, 5, 7]
let shared = oddDigits.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. intersection(_:) returns only members present in both Sets.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: union(_:) returns every member from either Set. Use intersection(_:) for shared members.

lessons.title: Set Difference Operations
lessons.objective: Return members that appear in exactly one of two Sets.
lessons.instruction: Exclude shared members and keep values unique to either Set.
lessons.codePrefix:
let a: Set = [1, 2, 3]
let b: Set = [3, 4]
let uniqueSides = a.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. symmetricDifference(_:) keeps members in either Set but not both.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: subtracting(_:) keeps only members from the receiver that aren't in the argument. Use symmetricDifference(_:).

lessons.title: Subset Membership
lessons.objective: Check whether every member of one Set appears in another.
lessons.instruction: Verify that all house animals are included among the farm animals.
lessons.codePrefix:
let house: Set = ["🐶", "🐱"]
let farm: Set = ["🐮", "🐔", "🐶", "🐱"]
let included = house.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. isSubset(of:) verifies that every house member belongs to farm.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: isSuperset(of:) checks the reverse relationship. Use isSubset(of:).
lessons.sourceTitle: Collection Types · Set Membership and Equality

lessons.title: Disjoint Sets
lessons.objective: Check whether two Sets share no members.
lessons.instruction: Verify that city animals and farm animals have no members in common.
lessons.codePrefix:
let city: Set = ["🐦", "🐭"]
let farm: Set = ["🐮", "🐔"]
let separate = city.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. isDisjoint(with:) returns true when the Sets have no common members.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: isStrictSubset(of:) checks containment. Use isDisjoint(with:) for no overlap.
lessons.sourceTitle: Collection Types · Set Membership and Equality

lessons.title: Dictionary and NSDictionary Bridging
lessons.objective: Recognize the Foundation class bridged with Swift Dictionary.
lessons.instruction: Choose the Foundation class that bridges with Swift Dictionary.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Swift Dictionary bridges with Foundation's NSDictionary class.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: NSArray represents an ordered collection. Swift Dictionary bridges with NSDictionary.
lessons.sourceTitle: Collection Types · Dictionary and NSDictionary Bridging

lessons.title: Dictionary Type Shorthand
lessons.objective: Declare key and value types with [Key: Value] syntax.
lessons.instruction: Declare airport codes mapped to airport names.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. [String: String] is shorthand for Dictionary<String, String>.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: [[String]] is an Array of Arrays. A Dictionary separates Key and Value with a colon.
lessons.sourceTitle: Collection Types · Dictionary Type Shorthand Syntax

lessons.title: Creating an Empty Dictionary
lessons.objective: Initialize an empty Dictionary with known key and value types.
lessons.instruction: Create an empty mapping from Int keys to String values.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. [:] is an empty Dictionary literal when the type supplies Key and Value.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: [] is an empty Array literal. Use [:] for an empty Dictionary.
lessons.sourceTitle: Collection Types · Creating an Empty Dictionary

lessons.title: Dictionary Literals
lessons.objective: Create key-value pairs with colon syntax.
lessons.instruction: Initialize YYZ with its airport name.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. The colon separates a Dictionary key from its value.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Comma-separated values form an Array. Use a colon for the key-value pair.
lessons.sourceTitle: Collection Types · Creating a Dictionary with a Dictionary Literal

lessons.title: Dictionary Subscripts Return Optionals
lessons.objective: Safely unwrap a value looked up by key.
lessons.instruction: Print the name only when the DUB key exists.
lessons.codePrefix:
let airports = ["DUB": "Dublin"]
if let name = airports[
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Dictionary lookup uses its Key type and returns an optional Value.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: This Dictionary's keys are String rather than integer positions. Look up "DUB".
lessons.sourceTitle: Collection Types · Accessing and Modifying a Dictionary

lessons.title: Updating a Dictionary Value
lessons.objective: Update a key while receiving its previous optional value.
lessons.instruction: Update DUB and bind the old airport name when it existed.
lessons.codePrefix:
var airports = ["DUB": "Dublin"]
if let oldName = airports.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. updateValue(_:forKey:) stores the new value and returns the previous value as an optional.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: removeValue(forKey:) deletes a pair. Use updateValue(_:forKey:) to replace and receive the old value.
lessons.sourceTitle: Collection Types · Accessing and Modifying a Dictionary

lessons.title: Removing a Dictionary Pair
lessons.objective: Remove a key-value pair and handle the optional removed value.
lessons.instruction: Remove DUB and enter the branch only when the key existed.
lessons.codePrefix:
var airports = ["DUB": "Dublin"]
if let removed = airports.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. removeValue(forKey:) deletes the pair and returns its former value or nil.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: updateValue requires a new value and preserves the key. Use removeValue(forKey:).
lessons.sourceTitle: Collection Types · Accessing and Modifying a Dictionary

lessons.title: Iterating over Dictionary Pairs
lessons.objective: Decompose each Dictionary element into key and value.
lessons.instruction: Choose the loop pattern that receives both airport code and name.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Dictionary iteration yields a (key, value) tuple for decomposition.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Each Dictionary element contains both key and value. Decompose it with (code, name).
lessons.sourceTitle: Collection Types · Iterating Over a Dictionary

levels.title: Level 5 · Control Flow
levels.summary: Repeat work, match patterns, exit early, and control scope cleanup.

lessons.title: For-In Loops
lessons.objective: Iterate over every element in a Sequence.
lessons.instruction: Bind and greet each name in the Array.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. for-in binds each value produced by the Sequence.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: where filters an existing pattern. Use in between the loop binding and Sequence.

lessons.title: For-In Dictionary Decomposition
lessons.objective: Decompose Dictionary elements inside a for-in loop.
lessons.instruction: Bind each animal name and leg count.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Dictionary iteration produces a key-value tuple for pattern decomposition.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Each element contains both key and value. Bind them with (animal, count).

lessons.title: Ignoring Loop Values
lessons.objective: Repeat work without binding an unused sequence value.
lessons.instruction: Multiply answer ten times without naming the range element.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. _ discards each produced value while preserving the repetition count.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: A named binding works but is unused. Use _ to express that the values don't matter.

lessons.title: Half-Open Strides
lessons.objective: Step through values without including the upper limit.
lessons.instruction: Generate minute marks 0 through 55 in steps of five, excluding 60.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. stride(from:to:by:) excludes the to value.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: through includes the upper value. Use to to stop before 60.

lessons.title: Closed Strides
lessons.objective: Step through values while including the final limit.
lessons.instruction: Generate hour marks 3, 6, 9, and 12.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. stride(from:through:by:) includes 12 when the sequence reaches it.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: to excludes the final limit. Use through to include 12.

lessons.title: While Loops
lessons.objective: Repeat only while a condition remains true.
lessons.instruction: Increment count until it reaches three.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. while checks its condition before each iteration.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: repeat begins an unconditional first iteration and needs a trailing while. Use while here.

lessons.title: Repeat-While Loops
lessons.objective: Execute a loop body at least once before checking its condition.
lessons.instruction: Perform the first attempt before deciding whether another attempt is required.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. repeat-while runs the body first and checks the condition afterward.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: A while loop requires its condition before the body. Use repeat with the trailing while condition.

lessons.title: If and Else
lessons.objective: Choose between two branches from a Boolean condition.
lessons.instruction: Use the cold branch at or below freezing and the alternative branch otherwise.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. else handles the values for which the if condition is false.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: default belongs to switch. Use else for the alternative if branch.

lessons.title: If Expressions
lessons.objective: Assign the value produced by an if expression.
lessons.instruction: Select one String expression and initialize advice directly.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Each if-expression branch produces the String used to initialize advice.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: guard performs early exit and isn't an expression here. Use if.

lessons.title: Switch Statements
lessons.objective: Match one value against exhaustive case patterns.
lessons.instruction: Choose the keyword that begins pattern matching for the Character.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. switch selects the first matching case and must cover every possible value.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: if needs a Boolean condition rather than case patterns. Use switch.

lessons.title: Switch Expressions
lessons.objective: Initialize a value from exhaustive switch branches.
lessons.instruction: Choose the expression keyword that produces message.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. The switch expression evaluates one branch and returns its String.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: case labels belong inside the construct. Begin the expression with switch.

lessons.title: Exhaustive Switch Matching
lessons.objective: Cover unmatched values with a default case.
lessons.instruction: Handle every Character not matched by a or z.
lessons.codePrefix:
switch letter {
case "a":
    print("First")
case "z":
    print("Last")
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. default matches all remaining values and makes the switch exhaustive.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: switch uses default rather than else for unmatched values.

lessons.title: No Implicit Fallthrough
lessons.objective: Match several values in one comma-separated case.
lessons.instruction: Match both lowercase and uppercase A without relying on fallthrough.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Comma-separated patterns share one body; Swift cases don't fall through implicitly.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Combine values in one case when they share behavior. Swift doesn't need C-style fallthrough here.

lessons.title: Interval Matching
lessons.objective: Match numeric values against range patterns.
lessons.instruction: Match every approximate count from 1 through 4.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. A range can act directly as a switch case pattern.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: An Array value isn't a pattern for these integers. Use the closed range 1...4.

lessons.title: Tuple Patterns in Switch
lessons.objective: Match selected tuple elements while ignoring others.
lessons.instruction: Match any point on the x-axis by requiring y to be zero.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. (_, 0) ignores x and requires the y coordinate to be zero.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: (0, _) matches the y-axis. Require the second element to be zero for the x-axis.

lessons.title: Switch Value Bindings
lessons.objective: Bind part of a matched tuple for use in the case body.
lessons.instruction: Match a point on the x-axis and capture its x coordinate.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. let binds the matched first element to x for the case body.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: An unbound x would be treated as an existing expression. Bind the matched value with let.

lessons.title: Switch Where Clauses
lessons.objective: Add a Boolean constraint to a bound case pattern.
lessons.instruction: Match points on the diagonal where both coordinates are equal.
lessons.codeSuffix:
x == y:
    print("On x == y")
default:
    break
}
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. where adds the x == y constraint after the value-binding pattern.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Case constraints use where rather than if.

lessons.title: Compound Cases with Shared Bindings
lessons.objective: Share one binding name across several case patterns.
lessons.instruction: Match either axis and bind its nonzero coordinate as distance.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. Every compound pattern binds distance with the same type so the body can use it.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: A compound case body needs the same bindings in every pattern. Bind distance in both.

lessons.title: If-Case Pattern Matching
lessons.objective: Run a branch only when a value matches a pattern.
lessons.instruction: Match points whose second coordinate is exactly 100 and bind x.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. if case applies one pattern without writing a full switch.
lessons.incorrectFeedback: Use if case for a single conditional pattern match.

lessons.title: For-Case Pattern Filtering
lessons.objective: Iterate only over sequence elements that match a pattern.
lessons.instruction: Visit only points on the x-axis and bind x.
lessons.correctFeedback: Correct. for case skips elements that don't match (let x, 0).
